content: 1. When estimating quantities and calculating nutrient profiles, foods were hydrated to water levels comparable to their boiled forms to ensure consistency in nutrient analysis. 2. Initially, all organ meats, seafood, and snails were included in the analysis. However, these items were excluded after reviewing draft nutrient profiles for subgroups, as they introduced bias into the nutrient profiles. 3. Insects were excluded from the analysis despite being identified as potentially nutrient-rich foods for infants and young children. This decision was based on the observation that insects were consumed by less than 5% of infants or children in the datasets analyzed. 4. Red palm oil was excluded from the subgroup of solid/saturated fats to prevent distortion of the nutrient profile for this category. 5. Rarely reported items that did not fit well into any subgroup and could bias subgroup nutrient profiles were excluded. Examples include hog bone marrow, toad meat powder, Vegemite/Marmite, and mung bean noodles. 6. Additional rarely consumed items that were nutrient outliers within their respective subgroups were also excluded. For example: Eel, which was very high in vitamin A and fat compared to other fish. Hawthorn fruit, which was extremely high in vitamin A, with concerns about the accuracy of its food composition data. 7. Whole grains and refined grains were operationally defined based on their carbohydrate-to-fiber ratio. Whole grain bakery items and breakfast cereals were defined as those with a carbohydrate-to-fiber ratio of ≤10:1. Refined grains included items with higher ratios. 8. Breakfast cereals were included in nutrient profile calculations if they contained ≤15 grams of total sugar per 100 grams, following the WHO Regional Office for Europe nutrient profile model for marketing to children. 9. Pseudocereals (e.g., amaranth, quinoa) and certain other grains (e.g., barley, teff, sorghum, millet) were grouped with whole grains unless specified as refined. 10. Sweet potatoes were classified based on their color and vitamin A content. In Southern Africa, unspecified sweet potatoes were assumed to be white-fleshed, while elsewhere, both white-fleshed and yellow/orange-fleshed varieties were included. 11. Fruits were categorized into subgroups such as vitamin A-rich fruits (e.g., mango, papaya), berries, citrus, vitamin C-rich fruits (e.g., guava, kiwi), bananas, high-fat fruits (e.g., avocado, coconut), and other fruits (e.g., apples, peaches). Vitamin A-rich fruits were defined per WHO/UNICEF guidelines, while vitamin C-rich fruits were defined as those containing ≥50 mg of ascorbic acid per 100 grams. 12. Vegetables were grouped into categories such as medium-to-dark green leafy vegetables, brassicas (e.g., broccoli, cabbage), vitamin A-rich orange vegetables (e.g., carrots, pumpkin), peppers and tomatoes, immature peas and beans, and other vegetables (e.g., onions, mushrooms). Specific groupings were based on nutrient content, plant part consumed, and dietary role. 13. Dairy products were categorized into milk, yogurt (including fermented dairy products like kefir), and cheese. Sweetened yogurts were included in quantity estimates but matched with unsweetened yogurts for nutrient profile calculations. 14. Protein sources were divided into subgroups such as eggs, legumes/pulses, soy foods, nuts/seeds, beef/lamb/goat, pork, poultry, liver, small fish eaten with bones, and larger fish not eaten with bones. Liver was separated from other organ meats due to its distinct nutrient profile, and seafood was excluded from modeling due to its rare consumption and disproportionate influence on nutrient profiles. 15. Data sources for modeling inputs included nationally representative datasets from various countries. These datasets were used to develop food item lists, maximum quantities for food subgroups, and allowed consumption frequencies. The datasets were selected based on criteria such as sample size, geographic representation, and availability of dietary intake information. 16. Specific challenges in data classification included distinguishing between whole and refined grains, grouping maize products, and classifying unspecified vegetables or legumes based on water and macronutrient content. This detailed explanation provides a comprehensive understanding of the methodology and decisions made in the analysis of food and nutrient data.
